prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as my preferred single-part prize, though after round 1 I hold it with less margin than before. The sequence is the one I trust: a specific, falsifiable prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011, flat bands at a magic angle) was followed by a clue from nature that nobody ordered, the correlated insulators and the superconducting dome near that angle (Cao et al. and the Jarillo-Herrero group, 2018). The central claims have been reproduced by independent groups and carried into other moire systems, including transition-metal dichalcogenides and fractional Chern states, so the discovery is not tied to one laboratory. To answer the chair directly: the pairing mechanism is a follow-up question, not part of what the prize would reward. The cuprates were honoured long before their mechanism was understood. What is rewarded is the prediction, the observation at the predicted angle and the new platform. The citation is worded to say exactly that and nothing about mechanism.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is maturity and credit. Eight years is short, the interpretation of the correlated states is still moving, and twist-angle disorder was a real limit on reproducibility in the early years. Credit is not airtight: Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 papers, falls outside three names, the earlier continuum-model work of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto is not credited, and Dean, Young, Yacoby, Efetov and Yazdani made decisive follow-ups. Mehlig's question about a two-theory, one-experiment split is fair; the split is defensible because the prediction and the observation are two distinct achievements inside one discovery, but it does leave a large part of the experimental community uncredited. Against that, the optical lattice clock (B012) has two cleanly separable names, a stable and quantitative result, and five colleagues behind it. If the committee judges that a prize should wait until the credit and the interpretation are cleaner, B012 is the defensible choice and I would not oppose it.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured different enabling tools, that a many-atom neutral lattice at the magic wavelength is a distinct achievement, and that the redefinition of the second is a consequence rather than a precondition.
responses.response: In round 1 I called the lattice clock an incremental step after the comb and the ion-control prizes. Having read Kroll, Olsson and Lindroth, I think that was too strong. The comb is a ruler and ion control is single-particle physics. The magic-wavelength lattice, which removes the trade-off between atom number and Doppler and recoil shifts and led to the 1e-18 regime, is a separate idea, and it brings in many-body effects that the single-ion clocks did not. I also accept his point that the SI redefinition is a consequence, not a precondition, so I withdraw that part of my objection. What remains of my reservation is only one of kind: B012 is a triumph of precision and control, whereas B042 is closer to a surprise from nature. That is a matter of taste for a theorist, not a defect in B012.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B012 first but says recognition of B042 may be slightly early because the superconductivity mechanism is unresolved, and asks whether the committee needs the mechanism settled before the topic stops counting as premature.
responses.response: My answer is no, the mechanism is not a precondition: the discovery is the flat-band prediction and the observation of correlated states and superconductivity at the predicted angle, and that has been reproduced across graphene and other moire systems. I concede that the test of stability she asks for is not yet fully met, since much of the later work is still being sorted out. Where I would like her help is the atomic-physics side of the competing case. You say that Ye's work is built on the comb. Is the strontium clock, the record systematics and the many-body clock work enough to count as a contribution that is distinct from the comb that earned the 2005 prize? If you tell the room plainly that it is, I will rank B012 level with B042 on credit.

responses.point: Mehlig supports B042 but says the interpretation of the correlated states is not yet stable and that the three-name limit leaves the broad experimental community uncovered, asking whether theory-two-experiment-one is the right allocation.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of his worry. On the Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto question, my reading is that they derived the continuum description and the velocity renormalisation, while Bistritzer and MacDonald located the magic angles and showed the band flatness that the experiments then targeted. That is why I credit Bistritzer and MacDonald, but I recognise it is a judgement a condensed-matter colleague should check. On the experimental side I do not think one name is arbitrary: Jarillo-Herrero led the group that made the observation and has continued as its principal driver. But I take his point seriously, and I would not call the allocation clean. That is the main reason that I now hold B042 only narrowly ahead of B012.

responses.point: Pearce, who moved to B012 after reading the openings, says the clock has two separable, documented contributions, and that he does not regard B042 as the more mature of the two.
responses.response: I agree that on maturity and cleanliness of credit, B012 is ahead, and I do not dispute it. Where I part from him is on what the committee weighs most. With two names who each have a documented, separable contribution, the clock is the safer prize. Yet the statutes ask for the most important discovery, and I would say a new class of correlated quantum matter, found where theory said to look, is at least as significant as a record in precision. I also note that on B035 we agree: one name for a collaboration of hundreds is not defensible and the sources of the diffuse flux are unidentified. I have no objection to his stepping back on B035 and B016 if they ever lead, since neither does.

responses.point: Olsson says that the lattice clock has a stable, quantitative result today, and that the 2005 comb prize honoured a tool, not the neutral-atom lattice idea; she ranks B042 second but is hesitant on maturity.
responses.response: I find her answer on the overlap convincing, as noted above. I disagree only with the implication that stability of the result is the deciding quality. What I would ask the committee is to consider the reverse risk. If we wait, B042 remains a young field that keeps maturing, and the experimental credit may become clearer or murkier, while the clock is a result that will still be just as sound next year. That asymmetry argues for taking B042 now only if we believe the credit can be written cleanly. If the room cannot agree on the allocation of the experimental credit, I will have no difficulty moving to B012 in the vote.

uncertainties: Whether three names can fairly represent B042 given Yuan Cao's role as first author of the 2018 experiments and the earlier continuum-model work of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto.
Whether eight years and a still-debated superconducting mechanism are enough maturity, compared with the settled and quantitative B012.

Whether Ye's contributions to the lattice clock are distinct enough from the comb work of 2005 to meet the overlap objection, and how much weight Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow deserve; I rely on Lindroth and Kroll for this.
For B016, whether the BeppoSAX team and the optical and radio followers can be separated fairly with three names; I keep it only as an alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict to report beyond round 1. My supervisor David Gross, my mentor Rubinstein and my co-author Van Riet are not credited in any shortlisted entry, and my own field of string theory and cosmology is distant from all candidates. I have no tie to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer.
